concepts.title: PRINT & COMMENTS
concepts.sub: print() puts text on the screen. Comments are notes Python ignores.
concepts.code:
print("Hello, World!")
print("Alice", "Bob", sep=" / ")
print("mango", end="!\n")
# This line is a comment - Python skips it
concepts.plain: print() shows whatever you put inside the parentheses. Commas print several things in a row, and sep / end change how those things are joined.
steps: Python sees print().
It reads the text inside the quotes.
It writes that text to the screen.

concepts.title: VARIABLES
concepts.sub: A variable is a name that points at a value you can reuse and change.
concepts.code:
name = "Alice"
age = 18
print(name, age)
age = 20
print(age)
concepts.plain: The = sign stores a value under a name. Writing the name later gives you the value back, and storing a new value replaces the old one.
steps: Choose a clear name.
Put = and the value after it.
Read the name anywhere below to get the value.

concepts.title: DATA TYPES
concepts.sub: Every value has a type: text, whole number, decimal, or True/False.
concepts.code:
name = "Alice"
age = 18
price = 9.99
is_adult = True
print(type(name), type(age))
print(type(price), type(is_adult))
concepts.plain: type() tells you what kind of value Python is holding. The type decides what you can do with it — math works on numbers, not on text.
steps: Pick a value.
Ask type(value).
Python names the type.

concepts.title: TYPE CONVERSION
concepts.sub: int(), float() and str() change one type into another.
concepts.code:
age_text = "10"
age = int(age_text)
print(age + 5)
print(str(age) + " years")
print(float(5))
concepts.plain: Text that looks like a number is still text. Convert it first with int() or float(), and the math finally works.
steps: Start with the value you have.
Wrap it in int(), float() or str().
Use the converted value from then on.

flow.title: FROM CODE TO SCREEN

steps.label: print("Hi")
steps.caption: You write a line of code.

steps.label: Python runs it
steps.caption: The interpreter works out the value.

steps.label: Hi
steps.caption: The text appears in the output.

flow.caption: Python reads the line, works out the value, then writes it to the screen.

mistake.why: Python is case-sensitive. print must start with a lowercase p, or Python looks for a variable called Print.

days.tip: Name variables after what they hold — price, not p. You will read your own code far more often than you write it.

lab.starter:
# Change these three lines, then press Run.
name = "Alice"
age = 18
city = "Lisbon"

print("Name:", name)
print("Age:", age, "->", type(age))
print("City:", city)
lab.hint: Try changing age to a text value like "18" and run again. What does type() say now?

checks.question: What does this line print?
checks.explain: sep is the separator placed between values, so the two letters are joined with a dash.

checks.question: Which line stores the number 42 as text?
checks.explain: Quotes make a value text. int("42") would convert it back into a whole number, and 42.0 is a float.

days.reflection: Which of the four types do you expect to use most in your own work — and what would you want to store with it?
recap: Print text, several values at once, and comments
Store values in clearly named variables
Identify str, int, float and bool
Convert between text, whole numbers and decimals
days.title: First Words
days.kicker: print(), variables, the four value types, and converting between them
days.goal: Make Python show something on screen, store your first values, and change one type into another.
days.task: Print your name, your age and your city — each stored in a variable first — then print the type of each value.

concepts.title: NUMBERS & MATH OPERATORS
concepts.sub: Python does real arithmetic with +, -, *, /, //, % and **.
concepts.code:
apples = 7
friends = 2
print(apples + friends)
print(apples // friends)
print(apples % friends)
print(apples ** 2)
print(10 / 4)
concepts.plain: Python reads arithmetic the way a calculator does. The two unusual signs are // for whole-number division and % for the remainder left behind.
steps: Put a number, an operator and another number.
Python works out the result.
print() shows it, or a variable keeps it for later.

concepts.title: STRINGS BASICS
concepts.sub: Text in quotes can be joined, repeated, measured and read by position.
concepts.code:
first = "Ada"
last = "Lovelace"
full = first + " " + last
print(full, len(full))
print("ha" * 3)
print("line one\nline two")
print(full[0], full[-1])
concepts.plain: A string is a row of characters with a number for each position, starting at 0. Plus joins strings, star repeats them, and square brackets pick one character out.
steps: Write the text inside quotes.
Join it with +, or repeat it with *.
Use [0] for the first character and [-1] for the last.

concepts.title: STRING METHODS
concepts.sub: Methods are actions attached to a string, called with a dot.
concepts.code:
raw = "  Green Tea  "
clean = raw.strip()
print(clean)
print(clean.upper())
print(clean.lower())
print(clean.replace("Green", "Black"))
print(clean.startswith("Green"))
concepts.plain: A method is a built-in action that belongs to the string. You write the string, a dot, the method name and parentheses, and you get a new string back.
steps: Start from the string you have.
Add a dot and the method name.
Put anything the method needs inside the parentheses.

concepts.title: F-STRINGS & FORMATTING
concepts.sub: An f-string puts values straight into a sentence and formats them.
concepts.code:
item = "coffee"
price = 4.5
qty = 3
total = price * qty
print(f"{qty} x {item} = {total:.2f} EUR")
print(f"{item.title()} costs {price:.2f} each")
print(f"Big order: {1234.5:,.2f} EUR")
concepts.plain: Put an f in front of the quotes, then write a name inside curly braces and Python drops its value into the text. A colon after the name adds formatting, such as .2f for two decimals.
steps: Put f just before the opening quote.
Write any name or expression inside curly braces.
Add :.2f or :, after a colon to control the look.

flow.title: TWO NUMBERS, ONE SENTENCE

steps.label: price * qty
steps.caption: An operator joins two numbers.
Python works out the value.

steps.label: 13.50 EUR
steps.caption: The f-string rounds and formats it.

flow.caption: Numbers are calculated first, then f-strings turn the result into readable text.

mistake.why: Plus cannot glue text to a number, but an f-string converts the number into text for you.

days.tip: Build every sentence with an f-string instead of gluing pieces with +, and your numbers will always look right.

lab.starter:
# A tiny receipt. Change the values, then press Run.
item = "  green tea  "
price = 3.5
qty = 4
clean = item.strip().title()
total = price * qty
print("ITEM:", clean)
print(f"Price: {price:.2f}")
print(f"{qty} x {clean} = {total:.2f}")
# Try qty = 0, or a name with no extra spaces.
lab.hint: strip() removes the spaces and title() fixes the capitals; you can chain both in one line.

checks.question: What does this line print?
checks.explain: // gives the whole number of times 2 fits into 7, and % gives what is left over.

checks.question: Which call turns "  Grace Hopper  " into "Grace Hopper"?
checks.explain: strip() removes the spaces at both ends and leaves the letters alone.

days.reflection: Which part of the receipt took longer to get right, the arithmetic or the formatting, and what did you change to fix it?
recap: Add, subtract, multiply and divide with Python operators
Use // for whole division and % for the remainder
Join, repeat and index strings
Clean text with strip(), upper(), lower() and replace()
Format numbers inside f-strings with .2f and thousands commas
days.title: Numbers & Text
days.kicker: math operators, string basics, string methods and f-strings
days.goal: Do real math with numbers, then shape text into the exact sentence you want.
days.task: Build a receipt: store a price and a quantity, print a total with two decimals in an f-string, and clean a messy product name into title case.

concepts.title: INPUT FROM THE USER
concepts.sub: input() asks a question and always hands back text.
concepts.code:
name = input("Name: ")
age = int(input("Age: "))
print("Hello,", name)
print("Next year you turn", age + 1)
# input() gives text, so int() is what makes the maths work
concepts.plain: The program pauses, shows the prompt and waits for Enter. Whatever the user typed arrives as a string, so wrap it in int() before you do arithmetic with it.
steps: Call input() with a short prompt.
Store the answer in a variable.
Convert it with int() or float() if you need numbers.

concepts.title: BOOLEANS & COMPARISONS
concepts.sub: A comparison asks a yes/no question and answers True or False.
concepts.code:
score = 72
pass_mark = 60
print(score > pass_mark)
print(score == 72)
print(score != 72)
print(score >= 90)
print("A" < "B")
concepts.plain: A single = stores a value, but == compares two values. Every comparison produces a bool, which is exactly what an if statement needs.
steps: Put one value on each side of the operator.
Read the answer: True or False.

concepts.title: IF / ELSE
concepts.sub: if runs a block only when its test is True; else covers the rest.
concepts.code:
balance = 40
price = 25
if balance >= price:
    balance = balance - price
    print("Bought it. Left:", balance)
else:
    print("Not enough money.")
print("Done")

notes.label: runs when the test is True
runs when the test is False
outside the if, so always runs

concepts.plain: The line ending in a colon opens a block, and the indented lines below it belong to that block. Exactly one of the two blocks runs, never both.
steps: Write if and a test, then a colon.
Indent the lines that belong to it.
Add else and another indented block for the other case.

concepts.title: ELIF CHAINS
concepts.sub: elif adds more tests, checked in order until one matches.
concepts.plain: Python walks down the chain and stops at the first True test, so order matters. Anything left over lands in the final else.
steps: Start with the strictest test.
Add elif lines for the middle cases.
Finish with else for everything else.

flow.title: FROM A TYPED ANSWER TO A BRANCH

steps.label: input("Age: ")
steps.caption: You ask the question in code.
The text becomes an int, ready to compare.

steps.label: Next year you turn 18
steps.caption: One branch runs and the other is skipped.

flow.caption: Ask, convert, compare: almost every interactive program follows this order.

mistake.why: input() hands back text, and Python cannot compare text with the number 18.

days.tip: Put your strictest test first: an elif chain stops at the first True, so a loose test near the top hides every branch below it.

lab.starter:
# A two-question quiz. Change the answers, then press Run.
name = input("Your name: ")
score = 0
answer = input("2 + 2 = ")
if answer == "4":
    score += 1
answer = input("Capital of France? ")
if answer.lower() == "paris":
    score += 1
print(name, "scored", score, "of 2")
if score == 2:
    print("Perfect!")
else:
    print("Try again.")
lab.hint: input() gives text, so compare it with "4" in quotes, or wrap it in int() and compare with 4.

checks.question: What does this print?
checks.explain: The text "10" is not the same value as the number 10, so the comparison is False.

checks.question: Which word appears?
checks.explain: The first test fails, the elif test passes, so only that block runs.

days.reflection: Think of one decision you made today. How would you write it as an if / elif / else chain, and what is the first test?
recap: Ask the user for a value with input()
Convert typed text with int() or float() before comparing it
Compare values to get True or False
Choose a branch with if / else
Chain more than two outcomes with elif
days.title: Asking & Deciding
days.kicker: input(), booleans, if / else, and elif chains
days.goal: Get answers from the user and let Python choose a different path for each one.
days.task: Write a three-question quiz with input() that greets the player by name at the end and prints a different message for each score band.

concepts.title: LOGICAL OPERATORS
concepts.sub: and, or and not combine simple tests into bigger ones.
concepts.code:
age = 25
has_ticket = True
print(age >= 18 and has_ticket)
print(age < 18 or has_ticket)
print(not has_ticket)
print(age >= 18 and not has_ticket)
concepts.plain: and is strict, so both tests must pass. or is generous, so one is enough, and not simply flips True into False.
steps: Write each test on its own first.
Join them with and or or.
Wrap a test in not when you need the opposite.

concepts.title: NESTED CONDITIONS
concepts.sub: An if inside an if lets the second question depend on the first.

notes.label: inner question, only if stock exists

concepts.plain: The inner block only gets a chance to run when the outer test was True. Each level adds one more indent, so the shape of the code shows the shape of the decision.
steps: Ask the big question in the outer if.
Indent one level and ask the smaller question.
Keep every deeper block four spaces further right.

concepts.title: FOR LOOP & RANGE()
concepts.sub: for repeats a block once for each value in a sequence.
concepts.plain: range() produces a run of numbers, and for hands them to your variable one at a time. The stop value is never included, which is why range(1, 4) counts 1, 2, 3.
steps: Choose a name for the loop variable.
Give for a sequence, such as range(1, 4).
Indent the lines that should repeat.

concepts.title: WHILE LOOP
concepts.sub: while repeats a block as long as its test stays True.
concepts.code:
fuel = 3
while fuel > 0:
    print("Laps left:", fuel)
    fuel -= 1
print("Tank empty")

notes.label: runs while the test is True
moves the loop toward its end

concepts.plain: while tests the condition first and runs the body only while it is True. Something inside the body has to change that condition, or the loop never stops.
steps: Set up a variable before the loop.
Write while and the test, then a colon.
Change the variable inside the body.

flow.title: ONE LINE, MANY PASSES

steps.label: for n in range(3):
steps.caption: One line stands in for three copies.

steps.label: n = 0, 1, 2
steps.caption: Python runs the body once per value.
Each pass prints its own result.

flow.caption: A loop is a promise: run this block again for every value in the sequence.

mistake.why: A loop header must end with a colon, or Python cannot tell where the body begins.

days.tip: Use for when you know how many repeats you need, and while when you are waiting for something to change.

lab.starter:
# The 5-times table. Change table to practise another one.
table = 5
for n in range(1, 6):
    print(table, "x", n, "=", table * n)
# A countdown that stops on its own.
start = 10
while start > 0:
    print("T-minus", start)
    start -= 1
print("Lift off")
lab.hint: range(1, 6) stops before 6, and the while loop ends the moment start is no longer above zero.

checks.question: What is printed?
checks.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    total += n
print(total)
checks.explain: range(1, 4) gives 1, 2 and 3, so total becomes 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

checks.question: What is printed?
checks.explain: n goes 3, then 1, then -1; the test fails only after n is already below zero.

days.reflection: Which job in your week repeats a known number of times, and which one is really a while loop waiting for something to change?
recap: Combine tests with and, or and not
Nest one if inside another and follow the indentation
Repeat work with for and range()
Repeat until a condition changes with while
days.title: Loops That Count
days.kicker: logical operators, nested conditions, for loops and while loops
days.goal: Combine conditions and repeat work without writing the same line twice.
days.task: Print the 5-times table with a for loop, then count down from 10 with a while loop — and skip the number 7 in both.

concepts.title: BREAK / CONTINUE / ELSE
concepts.sub: break leaves a loop, continue skips one pass, and else runs after a clean finish.
concepts.plain: continue jumps to the next pass, while break leaves the loop completely. The else block belongs to the loop and runs only when no break happened.
steps: Decide what should skip a pass and what should end the loop.
Use continue for the skip and break for the stop.
Add else only if you need to know the loop finished.

concepts.title: NESTED LOOPS
concepts.sub: A loop inside a loop handles rows and columns.

notes.label: prints after the inner loop ends

concepts.plain: The inner loop finishes completely for every single pass of the outer loop. That is how you build rows, tables and grids one piece at a time.
steps: Write the outer loop for the rows.
Indent an inner loop for the columns.
Indent the work one level deeper still.

concepts.title: LOOP PATTERNS
concepts.sub: Most loops are one of a few shapes: count, sum, find the best, build.
concepts.code:
prices = [4, 9, 2, 7]
total = 0
biggest = prices[0]
for p in prices:
    total += p
    if p > biggest:
        biggest = p
print("total:", total, "max:", biggest)
concepts.plain: An accumulator starts at zero and grows with every pass. A best-so-far variable starts at the first value and is replaced whenever something bigger turns up.
steps: Set a starting value before the loop.
Update it inside the loop for each item.
Print it once, after the loop has finished.

concepts.title: TERNARY & MATCH-CASE
concepts.sub: A ternary picks a value in one line, and match-case picks a branch from many.
concepts.code:
n = 7
label = "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"
print(n, "is", label)
match n:
    case 1 | 3 | 5 | 7:
        print("single digit odd")
    case _:
        print("something else")
concepts.plain: A ternary is a compact if / else that produces a value instead of running a block. match-case compares one value against a list of patterns and runs the first that fits.
steps: Write the value for True, then if, then the test, then else, then the other value.
For many branches, write match and the value.
Add one case per pattern and finish with case _.

flow.title: STOPPING EARLY

steps.label: for n in range(1, 8):
steps.caption: The loop starts counting.

steps.label: continue / break
steps.caption: A pass can skip ahead or end the loop.
Only the numbers that survived are printed.

flow.caption: break leaves the loop, continue skips one pass, and else runs only when no break fired.

mistake.why: Every case line ends with a colon, exactly like an if line, before its indented block.

days.tip: When a loop misbehaves, print the counter at the top of the body and the skipped or extra pass shows up immediately.

lab.starter:
# A grade calculator. Change score, then press Run.
score = 87

if score < 0 or score > 100:
    print("Not a real score")
else:
    match score // 10:
        case 10 | 9:
            print("A")
        case 8:
            print("B")
        case 7:
            print("C")
        case _:
            print("Keep practising")
lab.hint: score // 10 turns 87 into 8, so the case 8 branch is the one that runs.

checks.question: What is printed?
checks.explain: break stops the loop as soon as n reaches 3, so 3, 4 and 5 are never printed.

checks.question: Which statement skips the rest of this pass but keeps the loop running?
checks.explain: continue jumps straight to the next pass, while break leaves the loop for good.

days.reflection: Where could a break save your program from doing work it does not need to do?
recap: Leave a loop early with break and skip one pass with continue
Use the loop else to tell whether a break happened
Nest loops to build rows, tables and grids
Write short value choices with a ternary
Replace long elif chains with match-case
days.title: Loop Control
days.kicker: break, continue, nested loops, loop patterns, ternary and match-case
days.goal: Steer loops with break and continue, nest them, and compress long decisions.
days.task: Sum 1–100 with an accumulator, find the biggest value in [4, 9, 2, 7], then rewrite a grade calculator with match-case.

days.brief: Week 1 gave you print, variables, types, input, conditions and loops. This review asks you to combine all of them into one small program a stranger could actually play. Get the loop and the counter right and everything else is detail.
requirements: Store the secret number in a variable called secret before the loop starts, and keep it between 1 and 10.
Ask for a guess with input() inside a loop that keeps running until the guess matches secret.
Count every valid guess in a variable called tries, adding one per attempt.
Print "Higher" when the guess is below secret and "Lower" when it is above, and print neither on the winning guess.
Reject input that is not a whole number with a short message, then continue without crashing and without counting a try.
After the loop, print a closing message that includes the number of tries, for example "You got it in 3 tries."
days.starter:
# Week 1 review - the number-guessing game.
# The frame is here. Fill in every TODO and it plays.
secret = 7                    # the number to find, 1-10
tries = 0                     # how many guesses so far
guess = 0                     # the player's latest guess

print("I am thinking of a number from 1 to 10.")

while guess != secret:
    text = input("Your guess: ")

    # TODO 1: if text is not made of digits, print a warning
    #         and use continue so a bad guess is not counted.
    guess = int(text)

    # TODO 2: add one to tries.

    # TODO 3: print "Higher" when guess is below secret
    #         and "Lower" when guess is above it.
    if guess < secret:
        pass
    elif guess > secret:
        pass

# TODO 4: print a closing line that includes tries.
print("Game over.")
stretch: Cap the game at five tries: stop the loop when tries reaches 5 and print a different closing message when the player runs out.
Wrap the whole game in a while loop that asks Play again? (y/n) and resets tries at the start of every round.
Replace the fixed secret with a random one - read ahead to sheet 84 for random.randint(1, 10).

Can you store text, a whole number, a decimal and a True/False in clearly named variables?
Can you convert input() text into an int, and explain why the conversion is needed?
Can you do arithmetic with + - * / // % ** and predict what Python returns?
Can you build an f-string that shows a price with two decimals?
Can you write an if / elif / else chain that handles every case, including the leftovers?
Can you combine conditions with and, or and not without confusing yourself?
Can you write a while loop that stops on the right condition, and a for loop over range()?
days.reflection: Which part of the game did you rewrite most often - the loop, the counting, or the input check - and what made it finally work?
days.title: Review 1: Guess the Number

concepts.title: CREATING LISTS
concepts.sub: Square brackets hold an ordered row of values you can grow later.
concepts.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
scores = [42, 7, 95]
mixed = ["Ana", 31, True]
empty = []
print(fruits)
print(len(fruits), len(empty))

notes.label: a list with nothing in it

concepts.plain: A list is one name for many values, written between square brackets with commas in between. Python keeps them in the order you gave and counts them for you with len().
steps: Write the items inside [ ].
Separate them with commas.
Store the list in a variable and ask len() how many there are.

concepts.title: INDEXING
concepts.sub: A number in square brackets picks one item out of the list.
concepts.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date", "fig"]
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[2])
print(fruits[-1])
print(fruits[-2])
concepts.plain: An index is a position. Counting starts at 0, and a negative index counts backwards from the end, so -1 is always the last item.
steps: Count the positions from 0.
Put the position inside square brackets.
Use a negative number when you want to count from the end.

concepts.title: SLICING
concepts.sub: Two numbers and a colon cut out a whole section of a list.
concepts.code:
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
print(letters[1:4])
print(letters[:2])
print(letters[3:])
print(letters[::2])
concepts.plain: A slice takes a start and a stop separated by a colon. The start is included and the stop is not, and leaving a side empty means from the beginning or to the end.
steps: Pick where the slice starts.
Pick where it stops, remembering the stop is not included.
Leave a side empty when you mean the beginning or the end.

concepts.title: ADDING ITEMS
concepts.sub: append(), insert() and extend() make the same list longer.
concepts.code:
queue = ["Ana", "Ben"]
queue.append("Cleo")
queue.insert(0, "Dara")
queue.extend(["Eve", "Finn"])
print(queue)
print(len(queue))
concepts.plain: append() adds one item to the end, insert() puts one at a position you choose, and extend() adds every item of another list. The list changes in place, so no reassignment is needed.
steps: Decide where the new item belongs.
Call append(), insert() or extend().
Read the same variable again - the list itself has changed.

flow.title: BUILD, REACH, GROW

steps.label: fruits = [...]
steps.caption: You write the items in square brackets.
Python stores them in numbered slots.

steps.label: fruits[1:3]
steps.caption: An index or a slice reads the slots back.

flow.caption: A list is an ordered row of slots: brackets create it, numbers reach into it, and append() makes it longer.

mistake.why: A three-item list has indexes 0, 1 and 2. Index 3 is one past the end, so Python raises IndexError: list index out of range.

days.tip: Count from zero and let negative indexes do the work - fruits[-1] is the last item no matter how long the list grows.

lab.starter:
# Day 7 lab: five fruits, three slices, one new item.
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date", "elderberry"]

print("All:", fruits)
print("First:", fruits[0])
print("Last:", fruits[0])        # TODO 1: use a negative index

# TODO 2: print the middle three items with one slice.
print("Middle:", fruits[1:2])

# TODO 3: append "fig", then make this count say 6.
print("Count:", len(fruits))
lab.hint: A slice is start:stop and the stop is excluded, so the middle three of a five-item list are fruits[1:4].

checks.question: What does this print?
checks.explain: Negative indexes count from the end, so nums[-1] is 30, while nums[1] is the second item, 20.

checks.question: Which slice returns the last two items of a list called items?
checks.explain: items[-2:] starts two from the end and runs to the finish, while items[-1:] returns only the last item.

days.reflection: Think of a collection you handle every day - songs, receipts, chores. Which list operations would you reach for first, and why?
recap: Create lists with square brackets and count them with len()
Reach any item by index, including negative indexes from the end

concepts.title: REMOVING ITEMS
concepts.sub: remove() deletes by value, pop() by position, and clear() empties the list.
concepts.code:
queue = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"]
queue.remove("Ben")
print(queue)
last = queue.pop()
print(last, queue)
queue.clear()
print(queue)

notes.label: what was removed, what is left

concepts.plain: remove() finds a value and deletes its first appearance, pop() deletes by position and returns the item, and clear() throws everything away.
steps: Decide whether you know the value or the position.
Call remove(), pop() or del for one item, clear() for all of them.
Print the list to confirm what is left.

concepts.title: SORTING & REVERSING
concepts.sub: sort() reorders the list itself; sorted() returns a new one.
concepts.code:
scores = [42, 7, 95, 18]
scores.sort()
print(scores)
scores.sort(reverse=True)
print(scores)
print(sorted(scores))
print(sorted(["pear", "apple", "fig"]))
concepts.plain: sort() rearranges the list you call it on and returns None. sorted() builds a fresh list and leaves the original exactly as it was, and reverse=True flips either one.
steps: Call sort() when the list itself should change.
Add reverse=True for biggest first.
Call sorted() when the original order must survive.

concepts.title: SEARCHING
concepts.sub: The in test answers yes or no, index() gives a position, count() counts matches.
concepts.code:
names = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cleo", "Ben"]
print(names.index("Ben"))
print(names.count("Ben"))
print("Cleo" in names)
print("Dara" in names)
concepts.plain: Use in for a yes or no, index() for a position, and count() when duplicates matter. index() raises ValueError when the value is missing, so test with in first.
steps: Ask in when a True/False answer is enough.
Ask index() when you need the position.
Ask count() when the same value may appear more than once.

concepts.title: LOOPING LISTS & ENUMERATE()
concepts.sub: A for loop visits every item; enumerate() adds a counter beside it.
concepts.plain: A for loop hands you the items in order, one per pass. enumerate() hands you a counter and the item together, so you never have to track the number yourself.
steps: Loop over the list directly when you only need the items.
Wrap it in enumerate() when you also need a number.
Pass start=1 for numbering a human would recognise.

flow.title: TIDY, THEN NUMBER

steps.label: sort()
steps.caption: Python reorders the same list in place.

steps.label: in / index()
steps.caption: A search answers yes, or gives a position.

steps.label: 1. email
steps.caption: enumerate() adds a counter to every item.

flow.caption: Sort it, search it, then number it - three moves that turn a raw list into something readable.

mistake.why: remove() looks the value up before deleting it. If the value is not in the list, Python raises ValueError instead of quietly doing nothing.

days.tip: Never write scores = scores.sort(). sort() returns None, so that line keeps None and throws your list away - use sorted(scores) instead.

concepts.title: LIST COMPREHENSIONS
concepts.sub: One line builds a new list from an old one, with an optional filter.
concepts.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
doubled = [n * 2 for n in numbers]
evens = [n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
print(doubled)
print(evens)
print([word.upper() for word in ["hi", "bye"]])

notes.label: add if to keep only some

concepts.plain: A comprehension reads as what you want, then where it comes from, then which items to keep. It builds a brand new list and leaves the original alone.
steps: Write the expression you want for each item.
Add for name in list to walk the source.
Add if condition when only some items should survive.

concepts.title: COPYING & MUTABILITY
concepts.sub: Two names can point at one list, so changing it changes both.
concepts.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)
c = a.copy()
c.append(5)
print(a)
print(c)
concepts.plain: Assigning a list copies the name, not the list, so a change through one name shows up through the other. copy() makes a second list with the same contents.
steps: Notice that b = a creates an alias, not a copy.
Use a.copy() or list(a) when you need independence.
Change one list and print both to prove they are separate.

concepts.title: TUPLES
concepts.sub: A tuple is an ordered group that cannot be changed after it is built.
concepts.code:
point = (3, 5)
print(point)
print(point[0])
print(len(point))
single = (7,)
print(type(single))
concepts.plain: Tuples group values that belong together and should not change, like a coordinate or a date. Indexing and len() work exactly as they do for lists, but assignment does not.
steps: Write the values in parentheses.
Read them by index just like a list.
Remember the trailing comma for a one-item tuple.

concepts.title: TUPLE UNPACKING
concepts.sub: One assignment can pull a tuple apart into named variables.
concepts.code:
point = (3, 5)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
name, age, city = ("Ana", 31, "Lisbon")
print(name, city)
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(first, rest)
concepts.plain: Unpacking matches names on the left with values on the right, in order. The counts must agree unless one name has a star, which sweeps up whatever is left as a list.
steps: Count the values on the right.
Write the same number of names on the left.
Use a starred name when the tail can vary in length.

flow.title: ONE LINE, THREE PARTS

steps.label: for n in numbers
steps.caption: The loop visits every item.

steps.label: if n % 2 == 0
steps.caption: The filter keeps only what passes.
The expression builds the new list.

flow.caption: A comprehension packs a loop, a filter and a new list into one line you can read left to right.

mistake.why: Tuples are immutable: you cannot assign to a slot. Build a new tuple with the value you want instead.

days.tip: The comma makes a tuple, not the parentheses - (7) is just the number 7, while (7,) is a one-item tuple.

lab.starter:

# TODO 1: replace [] with a comprehension that doubles the even numbers.

copy = original.copy()
original.append(99)

# TODO 2: print both lists. Which one gained 99?

lab.hint: In a comprehension the expression comes first, then the loop, then the filter - and .copy() is what makes TODO 2 print two different lists.

checks.question: What does this print?
checks.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print([n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])
checks.explain: The if keeps only 2 and 4, then the expression squares each one, giving [4, 16].

checks.question: What does this print?
checks.explain: b = a copies the reference, not the list, so a and b are the same object and both show the appended 3.

days.reflection: Where in your own work would a fixed tuple be safer than a list - and what would you gain by making that data impossible to change?

Explain why b = a does not copy a list
Store fixed groups of values in tuples
Unpack tuples into named variables, with a star for the rest

concepts.title: SETS BASICS
concepts.sub: A set holds unique values and answers "is it in there?" instantly.
concepts.code:
numbers = {3, 1, 3, 2, 1}
print(len(numbers))
print(sorted(numbers))
print(4 in numbers)
empty = set()
print(empty, type(empty))
concepts.plain: Curly braces with values inside make a set, and Python quietly drops anything repeated. Sets have no order, so sort them when you want a predictable line.
steps: Wrap the values in curly braces.
Python keeps one copy of each value.
Use in to test membership, or len() to count.

concepts.title: SET OPERATIONS
concepts.sub: Union, intersection and difference compare two groups in one symbol.
concepts.plain: The pipe symbol joins two sets, the ampersand keeps what they share, and the minus sign removes one from the other. Each has a long method name that does exactly the same thing.
steps: Build the two sets you want to compare.
Pick | for both, & for shared, - for the leftover.
Sort the result before printing so the order is stable.

concepts.title: DICTIONARIES: CREATE & ACCESS
concepts.sub: A dictionary stores values under names instead of positions.
concepts.code:
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
print(person["name"])
print(person.get("city"))
print(person.get("city", "unknown"))
print(len(person))
concepts.plain: Square brackets fetch the value behind a key, but they demand that the key exists. get() asks politely and returns None, or whatever fallback you hand it.
steps: Write the pairs inside curly braces as key: value.
Read one with person[key] when the key must exist.
Use get(key, fallback) when it might not.

concepts.title: DICTIONARIES: ADD, UPDATE & DELETE
concepts.sub: Assign to a key to add or change it, and del to remove it.
concepts.code:
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
person["email"] = "alice@example.com"
person["age"] = 31
del person["email"]
print(person)
print(person.pop("age"))
print(person)
concepts.plain: A dictionary grows the first time you assign to a new key, and updates when the key already exists. del removes an entry silently, while pop removes it and hands the value back.
steps: Assign with person[new_key] = value to add.
Assign with person[old_key] = value to update.
Use del or pop when the entry should disappear.

flow.title: FROM LIST TO SET

steps.label: nums = [3, 1, 3, 2]
steps.caption: A list keeps every repeat, in order.

steps.label: set(nums)
steps.caption: Python builds a set and drops the duplicates.
One of each value is left, in no fixed order.

flow.caption: A set is the shortest route from a messy list to the unique values inside it.

mistake.why: Square brackets demand the key exists, while get() returns None instead of stopping the program.

days.tip: Reach for a set when you only care whether something is present, and a dictionary when each name needs a value attached to it.

lab.starter:
# Day 10 lab: clean a list, then grow a dictionary.

unique = set(numbers)
print("unique:", sorted(unique))

person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}

print("keys:", len(person))
lab.hint: A new key is just an assignment - person['email'] = 'a@b.com' - with no method needed.

checks.question: What does this print?
checks.explain: set() keeps one copy of each value and sorted() returns them as a list in ascending order.

checks.question: Which call returns None instead of raising KeyError when the key is missing?
checks.explain: get() returns None or your fallback when the key is absent, while square brackets and pop() raise KeyError.

days.reflection: Where in your own notes or files do you keep a list that is really a set of unique names, and what would a dictionary add to it?
recap: Build a set and explain why duplicates vanish
Compare sets with | & and -
Create a dictionary and read values with [] and get()
Add, update and delete dictionary entries

concepts.title: DICTIONARY METHODS
concepts.sub: keys(), values(), items(), get() and update() are the five you will use daily.
concepts.code:
scores = {"ann": 90, "bob": 75}
print(list(scores.keys()))
print(list(scores.values()))
print(scores.get("cid", 0))
scores.update({"cid": 88})
print(list(scores.items()))
concepts.plain: keys(), values() and items() give you a view of one dictionary from three angles. update() merges another dictionary in, replacing any key that already exists.
steps: Choose the view you need: keys, values or items.
Wrap it in list() when you want to print or index it.
Use update() to merge a second dictionary in one call.

concepts.title: LOOPING DICTIONARIES
concepts.sub: A loop over .items() hands you the key and the value together.
concepts.plain: Looping a dictionary directly gives you keys only. Add .items() when you need the value too, and unpack the pair into two variable names.
steps: Write for key, value in my_dict.items().
Use both names inside the loop body.
Loop .values() alone when you only need to total them.

concepts.title: NESTED DATA
concepts.sub: A list of dictionaries is the shape of almost every real record set.
concepts.code:
friends = [
    {"name": "Ann", "city": "Oslo"},
    {"name": "Bob", "city": "Lima"},
]
print(friends[1]["city"])
for friend in friends:
    print(friend["name"], "-", friend["city"])
concepts.plain: Reach into nested data one step at a time: friends[1] picks the second dictionary, and the second set of brackets picks a field inside it.
steps: Index the list to get one dictionary.
Index or get() that dictionary to get one field.
Loop the list to work on every record the same way.

concepts.title: CHOOSING A DATA STRUCTURE
concepts.sub: List, tuple, set or dict - pick by the question you need to ask.
concepts.code:
tags = ["python", "python", "sql"]
print(sorted(set(tags)))
point = (4, 7)
print(point[0] + point[1])
stock = {"apples": 3, "pears": 5}
print(stock["pears"])
concepts.plain: Lists keep order, tuples lock values together, sets guarantee uniqueness and dictionaries attach a value to a name. Choose the one whose question matches yours.
steps: Ask what you need: order, uniqueness, or lookup by name.
Pick the structure that makes that question one line.
Convert between them when the job changes.

flow.title: WALKING A DICTIONARY

steps.label: for k, v in d.items()
steps.caption: You ask for pairs, not just keys.

steps.label: each pair
steps.caption: Python hands over the key and its value together.

steps.label: ann 90
steps.caption: You print both halves on one line.

flow.caption: One dictionary becomes as many output lines as it has entries, one pair at a time.

mistake.why: Looping a dictionary yields keys only, so there is a single value to unpack where two names are waiting.

days.tip: When a dictionary surprises you, print list(my_dict.items()) - seeing key and value side by side explains most of it.

checks.question: Which expression gives you a printable list of a dictionary's values?
checks.explain: values() returns the values as a view, and list() turns that view into a list you can print.

concepts.title: DEFINING & CALLING
concepts.sub: def names a block of code, and the name plus () runs it.
concepts.code:
def greet():
    print("Hello!")

greet()
greet()
print("done")
concepts.plain: Defining a function only teaches Python the name; nothing runs until you call it. The indented body runs once per call, in order.
steps: Write def, the name, () and a colon.
Indent the lines that belong to the function.
Call it later by writing its name followed by ().

concepts.title: PARAMETERS & ARGUMENTS
concepts.sub: Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values you pass in.
concepts.code:
def greet(name, city):
    print("Hi", name, "from", city)

greet("Alice", "Lisbon")
greet(city="Oslo", name="Bob")
concepts.plain: Each argument fills one parameter. Pass them in order and they line up left to right, or name them and the order stops mattering.
steps: List the parameters inside the parentheses after def.
Call the function with one argument per parameter.
Use keyword arguments when the order is easy to forget.

concepts.title: RETURN
concepts.sub: return sends a value back to whoever called the function.
concepts.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(3, 4)
print(total)
print(add(10, 5) * 2)
print(add("py", "thon"))
concepts.plain: A returned value behaves exactly like the value you passed in: you can print it, store it or do math with it. The function stops at the return line.
steps: Compute the result inside the function.
Write return in front of it.
Use the call anywhere a value would fit.

concepts.title: DEFAULT & KEYWORD ARGUMENTS
concepts.sub: Defaults make arguments optional, and keywords name the one you mean.
concepts.code:
def order(item, qty=1, note="none"):
    return f"{qty} x {item} ({note})"

print(order("tea"))
print(order("coffee", 2))
print(order("cake", note="birthday"))
concepts.plain: A default is the value Python uses when you stay silent. Keyword arguments let you fill the third parameter while leaving the second one alone.
steps: Give the optional parameters a default with =.
Call with only the arguments you want to set.
Name a parameter to skip the ones before it.

flow.title: ONE NAME, MANY CALLS

steps.label: def area(w, h):
steps.caption: You name the job and its inputs.

steps.label: area(3, 4)
steps.caption: The call fills the parameters and runs the body.
return hands the answer back to the caller.

flow.caption: Write the steps once, then call the name whenever you need that answer again.

mistake.why: A function that only prints gives back None, so None + 1 later in your program raises TypeError.

days.tip: If you catch yourself copying the same three lines a second time, that is the moment to give them a name with def.

    print("area:", width * height)

area(3, 4)

# TODO 2: call area(10, 10) here, then call it once with keywords.

lab.hint: A function that prints has no value to give back; return is what lets the caller store or add the result.

checks.question: What does this print?
checks.explain: The first call uses the default b=2 and returns 6, while the second passes b=3 and returns 9.

checks.question: What does a function give back when no return statement ever runs?
checks.explain: Python returns None automatically when the function body ends without a return.

days.reflection: Which repeated block of code in your own work would you turn into a function first, and what would you name it?
recap: Define a function with def and run it by calling its name
Fill parameters with positional or keyword arguments
Send an answer back with return instead of printing it
Give parameters defaults and override only what you need
days.title: Your Own Functions
days.kicker: defining, calling, parameters, return values and defaults
days.goal: Package code into functions with parameters, return values and sensible defaults.
days.task: Write area(width, height) and use it for three rectangles — then call it once with a keyword argument.

concepts.title: *ARGS & **KWARGS
concepts.sub: *prices collects extra positional arguments; **info collects extra keywords.
concepts.plain: *args and **kwargs let one function accept whatever you pass it. The single star packs the extra values into a tuple, the double star packs the extra keywords into a dictionary.
steps: Put * before a parameter name to gather extra positional arguments into a tuple.
Put ** before a parameter name to gather extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.
Read them inside the function like any other tuple or dictionary.

concepts.title: SCOPE
concepts.sub: Names created inside a function live only inside that function.
concepts.code:
count = 10

def show():
    count = 3
    print("inside", count)

show()
print("outside", count)
concepts.plain: Python looks for a name inside the function first, then outside it. An assignment inside the function creates a local name and leaves the outside one exactly as it was.
steps: Python checks the local names first, then the global ones.
An assignment inside a function creates a local name, even when a global has the same name.
Return the new value instead of editing the global one.

concepts.title: LAMBDA FUNCTIONS
concepts.sub: A lambda is a one-line function you can pass straight into another call.
concepts.code:
double = lambda n: n * 2
print(double(7))

pairs = [("tea", 3), ("coffee", 1), ("juice", 2)]
pairs.sort(key=lambda item: item[1])
print(pairs)
concepts.plain: A lambda is a tiny function written on one line: parameters, a colon, then a single expression that becomes the return value. It is handy when you need a function once, right where you use it.
steps: Write lambda, then the parameters, then a colon.
Put one expression after the colon - that value is returned.
Pass it where a function is expected, such as the key of sorted() or sort().

concepts.title: BUILT-IN FUNCTIONS
concepts.sub: Python ships with ready-made functions for counting, comparing and reshaping.
concepts.code:
numbers = [4, 9, 2, 7]
print(len(numbers), max(numbers), min(numbers))
print(sum(numbers), round(3.14159, 2))
print(sorted(numbers))
print(list(map(str, numbers)))
concepts.plain: len, max, min and sum answer questions about a collection in one call. round, sorted and map reshape values without you writing a loop.
steps: Pick the built-in that answers your question.
Pass the collection inside the parentheses.
Store or print the result - the original list is unchanged.

flow.title: ONE FUNCTION, MANY SHAPES

concepts.sub: Say what a function does, and label what goes in and what comes out.

concepts.title: RECURSION BASICS
concepts.sub: A recursive function solves a small piece and hands the rest to itself.

notes.label: a smaller copy of the job

concepts.plain: A recursive function calls itself with a slightly smaller input until it reaches a case it can answer directly. That smallest case is the base case, and without it the calls never stop.
steps: Find the smallest input you can answer immediately.
Return that answer without calling yourself - this is the base case.
For everything else, call yourself with a smaller input and combine the result.

concepts.title: STRING SLICING
concepts.sub: A slice cuts a piece out of a string using start, stop and step.
concepts.code:
word = "keyboard"
print(word[0:3])
print(word[3:])
print(word[-4:])
print(word[::-1])
print(word[::2])
concepts.plain: The number before the colon is where the slice starts, the number after is where it stops without being included, and a third number is the step. Negative numbers count from the end, so -1 is the last character.
steps: Write word[start:stop] and remember stop is not included.
Leave one side empty to run to the beginning or the end.
Add a second colon and a step, such as [::-1], to skip characters or reverse.

concepts.title: SPLIT() & JOIN()
concepts.sub: split() turns text into a list of pieces; join() glues a list back into text.

sentence = "the quick brown fox"
words = sentence.split()
print(words)
print(len(words))
print("-".join(words))
print(" ".join(["a", "b", "c"]))
concepts.plain: split() cuts a string into a list at every space, or at whatever character you pass in. join() walks a list and glues the pieces together with the separator you chose.
steps: Call split() with no argument to break on any run of spaces.
Pass a character, such as a comma, when your text is separated that way.
Call separator.join(list) to put the pieces back together.

concepts.title: FIND & REPLACE
concepts.sub: Locate a piece of text, count it, or swap it for something else.

text = "the cat sat on the mat"

print(text.count("the"))
print(text.replace("cat", "dog"))
print(text.find("zebra"))
out: the dog sat on the mat
concepts.plain: find() returns the position where a piece of text starts, or -1 when it is not there at all. replace() returns a new string with every match swapped out, and the original text never changes.
steps: Call find() and check that the result is not -1.
Call replace() with what to look for and what to put instead.
Store the returned string, because the original stays as it was.

concepts.title: CASE & WHITESPACE
concepts.sub: Trim the edges, change the case, and make names look tidy.
concepts.code:
raw = "  Ada Lovelace  "
clean = raw.strip()
print(clean)
print(clean.lower())
print(clean.upper())
print("Mixed Case".swapcase())
print("hello world".title())
concepts.plain: strip() removes spaces from both ends, lower() and upper() change the case of every letter, and title() capitalises each word. Every one of them returns a new string.
steps: strip() the raw text first - it is usually the very first step.
Lower both sides when you want a case-insensitive comparison.
Use title() when the text is going on screen for a person to read.

concepts.title: ESCAPE CHARACTERS & MULTILINE
concepts.sub: A backslash lets you type quotes, tabs and line breaks inside a string.
concepts.code:
print("She said \"hi\"")
print("Line one\nLine two")
print("C:\\Users\\ada")
print("""First
second""")
concepts.plain: A backslash changes the character that follows it: \" puts a real quote inside a string, \\ is a literal backslash, and \n starts a new line. Triple quotes keep a block of text exactly as you typed it.
steps: Put a backslash before a quote when the string is wrapped in that same quote.
Use \n inside a string for a line break and \t for a tab.
Use triple quotes when the line breaks should fall exactly where you typed them.

concepts.title: READING FILES
concepts.sub: Open a text file and walk through it one line at a time.
concepts.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("milk\neggs\nbread\n")

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

notes.label: three lines, each ending in a newline

concepts.plain: open() hands you a file object, and looping over it gives you one line at a time, newline included. That is why you strip() each line before printing or comparing it.
steps: Open the file with open(name) - read mode is the default.
Loop over the file object, or call read() to get the whole file at once.
strip() the trailing newline before you use the text.

concepts.title: WRITING FILES
concepts.sub: Write text to disk so it is still there after the program ends.
concepts.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("milk\n")
    f.write("eggs\n")

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

notes.label: newline, or the lines run together

concepts.plain: Opening a file with "w" creates it, or empties it if it already exists, and write() puts text inside. Nothing appears on screen - you have to open the file again to see what you saved.
steps: Open the file in write mode with open(name, "w").
Call write() with the exact text you want, including \n where the lines should break.
Let the with block end so the text actually reaches the disk.

concepts.title: THE WITH STATEMENT
concepts.sub: with opens a file and guarantees it gets closed again.
concepts.code:
with open("diary.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Monday: rain\n")

with open("diary.txt") as f:
    print(f.readline().strip())
print("closed:", f.closed)
concepts.plain: with opens the file, gives it a name inside the block, and closes it automatically when the block ends - even if something goes wrong inside. You never have to remember close().
steps: Write with open(...) as name: on one line.
Indent everything you want to do while the file is open.
Dedent - at that point the file is closed for you.

concepts.title: PATHS WITH PATHLIB
concepts.sub: Build and inspect file paths as objects instead of raw strings.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("data")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
file = folder / "log.txt"
file.write_text("started\n")
print(file.name, file.suffix)
print(file.exists())
concepts.plain: Path turns a plain string into a path object. The / operator joins folder and file names, and the object knows its own name, its suffix and whether it exists.
steps: Build a Path from a string.
Join more parts with the / operator.
Ask the path questions, or call write_text() to save in one step.

concepts.title: CSV & JSON BASICS
concepts.sub: Two plain-text formats: rows of cells, and shaped data.

with open("scores.csv") as f:
    rows = list(csv.reader(f))
print(rows, json.dumps({"Ada": 95}))
concepts.plain: CSV is rows of comma-separated text, which is exactly what a spreadsheet wants. JSON keeps the shape of lists and dictionaries as text, so it can be loaded back as real Python objects.
steps: Write CSV rows with csv.writer, and pass newline="" when you open the file.
Read CSV with csv.reader - every cell comes back as a string.
Turn Python data into JSON text with json.dumps, and back with json.loads.

concepts.title: READING A TRACEBACK
concepts.sub: The last line names the error; the lines above show how Python got there.
concepts.plain: A traceback is a report, not noise. Read the bottom line first because it names the error, then walk up to the file line where Python stopped.
steps: Read the last line for the error type and message.
Find the line number just above it: that is where Python stopped.
Walk up the frames to see which call led there.
Fix the earliest real cause, then run again.

concepts.title: SYNTAXERROR VS RUNTIME
concepts.sub: A syntax error stops Python before any line runs; a runtime error happens mid-run.
concepts.plain: Python checks the whole file for syntax first, so a missing colon or bracket stops everything before line one. A runtime error only appears when a line actually runs.
steps: Python parses the whole file before it runs anything.
A SyntaxError stops the run with no output at all.
A runtime error appears later, when the failing line finally runs.

concepts.title: TRY / EXCEPT
concepts.sub: Wrap the risky line in try, then say what to do in except.
concepts.code:
text = "twelve"
try:
    number = int(text)
    print("Converted:", number)
except ValueError:
    print("That was not a number:", text)
print("Program keeps going")
out: That was not a number: twelve
concepts.plain: try says watch this block. If an error appears, Python skips the rest of the block and runs the matching except instead of crashing.
steps: Put the risky lines under try:.
Name the error you expect in except.
Handle it, then let the program continue.

concepts.title: CATCHING SPECIFIC ERRORS
concepts.sub: Name each error you can handle, and let the ones you cannot handle crash.
out: cannot divide by zero numbers only
concepts.plain: Python tries each except clause in order and runs the first one that matches. Catching named errors keeps real bugs visible, while a bare except hides them.
steps: List the errors you can actually fix.
Write one except per error, most specific first.
Let anything else crash so you can see it.

concepts.sub: Print the values you are unsure about, or pause the program and inspect them.

concepts.title: METHODS & SELF
concepts.sub: A method is a function inside a class, and self is the object it was called on.
concepts.plain: A method is just a function written inside the class body. Its first parameter, self, is the object the method was called on, so describe() can read that book's own title and pages without you passing anything in.

concepts.title: __STR__ & __REPR__
concepts.sub: print(obj) uses __str__, while repr(obj) and lists use __repr__.
concepts.plain: Without these two methods, print shows a memory address like <__main__.Book object at 0x10f3a2c>. __str__ is the friendly line for people; __repr__ is the exact version you want in a list or a traceback.

Return a precise, rebuildable string from __repr__.

concepts.title: CLASS VS INSTANCE ATTRIBUTES
concepts.sub: A class attribute is shared by every object; an instance attribute belongs to one.

class Book:
    library = "City Library"
    def __init__(self, title):

a = Book("Dune")
b = Book("Emma")
a.library = "Home Shelf"

concepts.plain: library is written once on the class, so every Book reads the same value. Assigning a.library gives that one object its own attribute, which hides the class value, while b keeps reading the original.

concepts.title: INHERITANCE
concepts.sub: class EBook(Book) reuses everything Book has and adds its own methods.
concepts.plain: The parent class goes in the brackets. EBook never writes __init__, yet EBook('Dune') still stores a title because Book's version runs, and isinstance() confirms that a subclass counts as its parent.

concepts.title: SUPER()
concepts.sub: super() calls the parent's version of a method instead of copying it.
concepts.plain: super() gives you the parent object, so super().label() runs Book's version and hands its result back to you. You extend that result instead of repeating the parent's code inside the subclass.

concepts.title: PROPERTIES & ENCAPSULATION
concepts.sub: A property looks like an attribute but runs a method every time you read it.
concepts.plain: The @property decorator turns a method into something you read without brackets, and the calculation runs fresh each time. Add a setter and the object can reject bad values before they are stored — that is encapsulation.

concepts.title: DUNDER METHODS
concepts.sub: Double-underscore methods let your object plug into len(), == and print().
concepts.plain: len(obj) looks for __len__, the == operator looks for __eq__, and print() looks for __str__. Define them and your objects behave like built-in values instead of comparing memory addresses.

Define the matching dunder method with the right parameters.
Use the normal syntax — Python finds the method for you.

concepts.title: DATACLASSES
concepts.sub: @dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from typed fields.

from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass

    title: str
    pages: int = 100
b = Book("Dune")
print(b)
print(b == Book("Dune", 100))
concepts.plain: One decorator replaces the boilerplate: each typed field becomes an __init__ parameter, defaults work, and __repr__ and __eq__ are written for you.
steps: Import dataclass from the dataclasses module.

concepts.title: IMPORT
concepts.sub: import loads a module; from ... import takes one name out of it.
concepts.code:
import math
from math import pi
import datetime as dt
print(math.floor(3.7))
print(round(pi, 2))
print(dt.date(2025, 1, 1).year)
concepts.plain: import math puts the whole module in your file and you reach inside with a dot. from math import pi copies just that one name, and as dt renames a module so long names stay readable.
steps: Write every import at the top of the file.
Reach the contents with module.name.
Use from ... import name when you only need one tool.

concepts.title: YOUR OWN MODULES
concepts.sub: Any .py file in the same folder can be imported by its filename.
concepts.code:
# dice.py
def double(n):
    return n * 2

# main.py
from dice import double
print(double(21))
concepts.plain: Save these as two files side by side: dice.py holds the function, main.py imports it. The filename without .py is the module name, so the import is simply dice, and Python finds it in the same folder.
steps: Create dice.py with a function at the top level.
Create main.py beside it and import dice.
Run main.py from that folder.

concepts.title: MATH
concepts.sub: math adds roots, rounding, constants and number theory to plain arithmetic.
concepts.code:
import math
print(math.sqrt(144))
print(math.floor(3.9), math.ceil(3.1))
print(math.pi)
print(math.gcd(12, 18))
concepts.plain: math covers what the operators do not: sqrt returns a float even for perfect squares, floor and ceil round down and up to whole numbers, and gcd finds the largest shared divisor.
steps: import math at the top of the file.
Call math.name(...) for the tool you need.
Expect a float from sqrt, so format it before printing if you want two decimals.

concepts.title: RANDOM
concepts.sub: random picks numbers and items; seed() makes those picks repeatable.
concepts.code:
import random
random.seed(7)
print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(random.choice(["red", "green", "blue"]))
cards = ["A", "K", "Q"]
random.shuffle(cards)
print(cards)
concepts.plain: randint includes both ends, choice takes one item from a sequence, and shuffle reorders a list in place without returning a new one. seed() fixes the sequence, so the same script prints the same values twice.
steps: import random at the top of the file.
Pick a value with randint, choice or shuffle.
Call seed() first whenever you need repeatable results.

concepts.title: DATETIME
concepts.sub: datetime stores a date and a time together, and timedelta moves it forward or back.
concepts.code:
from datetime import datetime, date, timedelta

start = datetime(2026, 11, 23, 9, 30)
print(start)
print(start.strftime("%d %b %Y"))
print(start + timedelta(days=7))
print(date(2026, 12, 25).weekday())
concepts.plain: A datetime holds a year, month, day, hour and minute in one value. strftime() turns that value into the text you want, and timedelta() adds or subtracts a span of time.
steps: Build the moment with datetime(2026, 11, 23, 9, 30).
Print it directly, or shape it with strftime().
Move it with + timedelta(days=7).

concepts.title: OS & SYS
concepts.sub: os works with paths and files, while sys tells you about the running Python.
concepts.code:
import os
import sys

print(os.path.basename("/home/ana/notes.txt"))
print(os.path.join("data", "2026", "notes.txt"))
print(os.path.splitext("report.csv"))
print(os.path.exists("/definitely/missing.txt"))
print(sys.version_info.major)
concepts.plain: os.path knows how paths are built on the machine you are on, so you never glue folder names together with slashes by hand. sys holds facts about the interpreter itself, like its version and the arguments it was started with.
steps: Import os for paths and sys for interpreter facts.
Ask os.path to split or join a path.
Read a sys attribute such as version_info.

concepts.title: TIME
concepts.sub: time measures how long code takes with perf_counter() and formats moments with strftime().
concepts.code:
import time

start = time.perf_counter()
total = sum(range(100_000))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(total, round(elapsed, 6) >= 0)
print(time.strftime("%A", time.gmtime(86400)))

notes.label: a timestamp as a day name

concepts.plain: perf_counter() is a precise stopwatch: read it before and after the work, then subtract to get the seconds. time.strftime() turns a timestamp into text, and gmtime(86400) is one day after 1 January 1970.
steps: Take a perf_counter() reading before the work.
Take another reading after it.
Subtract the two, then format any timestamp with strftime().

concepts.title: COLLECTIONS
concepts.sub: Counter counts things for you, and defaultdict fills in a missing key automatically.
concepts.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

tally = Counter("ana ben ana cara ana ben".split())
print(tally["ana"], tally["dan"], tally.most_common(1))

by_team = defaultdict(list)
by_team["blue"].append("ana")
print(dict(by_team))
concepts.plain: Counter turns any collection into counts, and asking for a name it has never seen returns 0 instead of crashing. defaultdict calls a factory when a key is missing, so you can append to a list that did not exist yet.
steps: Build the Counter from a list or a string.
Read counts by key, including keys that come back as 0.
Use defaultdict(list) when you group items under a label.

concepts.title: ITERTOOLS
concepts.sub: itertools builds ready-made loops: every combination, an endless cycle, and a safe slice of it.
concepts.code:
from itertools import combinations, cycle, islice

for pair in combinations(["ana", "ben", "cara"], 2):

concepts.plain: combinations() gives you every pair from a list without writing two nested loops. cycle() repeats its input forever, so islice() is how you take a fixed number of items from something endless.

concepts.sub: A readable program is constants on top, small functions in the middle, one entry point at the bottom.

concepts.sub: A menu is a loop that reads a choice, acts on it, and stops when the user quits.
concepts.plain: The loop keeps asking until the choice is q, so a wrong key just prints a hint and asks again. Anything typed by the user is text, so compare it with text like '1', never with the number 1.

concepts.title: WORKING WITH APIS
concepts.sub: An API is a URL that answers with data instead of a web page.
concepts.code:
import json, urllib.request

url = "https://api.github.com/repos/python/cpython"
# requests: pip install requests, then requests.get(url, timeout=10).json()
with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) as reply:
    data = json.load(reply)

print(data["name"], data["stargazers_count"])
concepts.plain: An API returns JSON text that your program can turn into a dictionary. requests is the friendliest way to call one (pip install requests first); urllib.request does the same job with nothing to install.
steps: Pick the endpoint and add a timeout.

Parse the JSON body, then read the fields you need.

concepts.title: REGEX BASICS
concepts.sub: A regex is a pattern for text: which characters, and how many of them.
concepts.code:
import re

text = "Ana: ana@mail.com, Ben: ben@site.org"
emails = re.findall(r"[\w.]+@[\w.]+", text)
print(emails)
print(re.sub(r"\d+", "#", "Room 12, floor 3"))
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{3}-\d{4}", "555-1234")))
concepts.plain: re.findall() returns every piece of text that matches the pattern, re.sub() replaces each match, and re.fullmatch() checks that the entire string fits. The r before the quotes keeps every backslash exactly as written.
steps: Write the pattern as a raw string, r'...'.
Choose findall, sub or fullmatch for the job.
Print the result, then tighten the pattern.

concepts.title: COMPREHENSION PATTERNS
concepts.sub: The same one-line pattern builds lists, sets and dictionaries, with an optional if.
concepts.plain: Read a comprehension from the middle out: for each item, keep it if the condition passes, then transform it. Swap the brackets and you swap the container you get back.
steps: Start from the for clause.
Add an if to filter.
Choose brackets: [] for a list, {} for a set or a dict.

concepts.title: GENERATORS & YIELD
concepts.sub: yield turns a function into a generator that produces one value each time you ask.
concepts.code:
def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1

print(list(countdown(3)))
gen = countdown(2)
print(next(gen), next(gen))
concepts.plain: A generator does not build the whole list up front; it pauses at each yield and resumes when you ask for the next value. That is why it can stream a million records without holding them all in memory.

concepts.sub: A decorator takes a function and hands back a wrapped version of it.
concepts.plain: A decorator is a function that wraps another function. The @ line runs once, at definition time: it calls shout(greet) and rebinds the name greet to the returned wrapper. From then on, greet() runs the wrapper, which runs your original code and adds something to the result.

concepts.title: CLEAN CODE (PEP 8)
concepts.sub: PEP 8 is Python's shared style guide for names, spacing and line length.
concepts.code:
def make_label(name, done):
    """Return a short status label."""
    status = "done" if done else "open"
    return f"[{status}] {name}"


print(make_label("buy milk", False))
print(make_label("walk dog", True))
concepts.plain: PEP 8 does not change what your code does, only how fast a human can read it. Lowercase words joined by underscores for functions and variables, UPPER_CASE for constants, four spaces per indent, two blank lines between top-level functions, and lines short enough to read without scrolling sideways.
steps: Name things for a reader: total_price, not tp.

days.brief: Thirty days ago you printed one line of text; today you ship a program. The To-Do CLI is small enough to finish in one sitting and real enough to keep on your own machine: it stores your tasks, remembers them between runs, and refuses to crash when you type nonsense. Every part of the course meets here - lists and dictionaries, functions, files and JSON, try/except, a menu loop, classes if you want them, and PEP 8 - which is exactly what makes it a fair final exam. Build it, run it, break it, then fix it.
requirements: Add a task: menu choice 1 asks for a title and appends a dict with that title and done set to False.
List tasks: menu choice 2 prints every task as 1. [ ] title, shows an x inside the brackets when done is True, and prints a friendly line when there is nothing to show.
Mark done: menu choice 3 asks for the number printed by list and sets that task's done to True, then saves.
Remove a task: menu choice 4 asks for a number and deletes that task from the list, then saves.
Persist: write the list to tasks.json with json.dump(..., indent=2) after every change, and load it again on start, beginning from an empty list when the file does not exist yet.
Menu loop: keep showing the menu and asking for a choice until the user picks 5, then save once more and exit cleanly.
Bad input never crashes: a non-number, an out-of-range index or an unknown menu choice prints one short message and returns to the menu instead of raising an exception.
Structure: one function per command, all called from main(), which sits under if __name__ == "__main__":, with no work happening at import time.
stretch: Due dates: store an ISO date string per task and print every task dated before datetime.date.today() as overdue.
Priorities: add a 1 to 3 priority field and sort the open tasks so 1 prints first.
Search: add choice 6 that prints every task whose title contains a keyword, ignoring capital letters.
Edit: add choice 7 that replaces the title at a given index while keeping that task's done state.
